lessons.title: Read a fraction as equal parts
lessons.idea: A fraction names some equal parts of a whole.
body: The bottom number tells how many equal parts make the whole. The top number tells how many parts we choose. Equal-sized parts let us compare amounts fairly.

equationGuide.meaning: The bottom number tells how many equal parts make the whole. The top number tells how many parts we choose. Equal-sized parts let us compare amounts fairly.

example.title: Three parts of one sheet
steps: Fold a sheet into 4 equal parts.
Colour 3 of those parts. The coloured share is 3/4.

lessons.terms: Fraction: A number written as one number divided by another. Numerator: The top number: the chosen parts in this example. Denominator: The bottom number: equal parts in the whole in this example.

glossary.definition: A number written as one number divided by another.
The top number: the chosen parts in this example.
The bottom number: equal parts in the whole in this example.

lessons.limits: The denominator cannot be zero. This first example uses parts of one whole; fractions can also be greater than one.

focus.idea: A fraction names some equal parts of a whole.
focus.explanation: The bottom number tells how many equal parts make the whole. The top number tells how many parts we choose. Equal-sized parts let us compare amounts fairly.

example.title: Three parts of one sheet
steps: Fold a sheet into 4 equal parts.
Colour 3 of those parts. The coloured share is 3/4.

terms.definition: A number written as one number divided by another.
The top number: the chosen parts in this example.
The bottom number: equal parts in the whole in this example.

check.prompt: A ribbon has 5 equal pieces. You keep 2. Which fraction is yours?
explanations: Yes. You kept 2 of the 5 equal pieces.
The whole has 5 pieces, so 5 belongs on the bottom.
Use the original 5 pieces as the whole.

apply.title: Try the same idea with a new value
apply.text: A shape has 8 equal parts and 3 are shaded. In 3/8, what is the denominator?
apply.answer: The denominator is 8: the number of equal parts in the whole.

parts.feedback: The denominator is 8: the number of equal parts in the whole.

lessons.title: Read hundredths in a decimal
lessons.idea: A decimal can name parts smaller than one.
body: The first place after the decimal point counts tenths. The next counts hundredths. One hundredth is one of 100 equal parts of one.

equationGuide.meaning: The first place after the decimal point counts tenths. The next counts hundredths. One hundredth is one of 100 equal parts of one.

example.title: Twenty-five small squares
steps: Divide one square into 100 equal small squares.
Shade 25 of them. The shaded share is 25/100, written 0.25.

lessons.terms: Decimal point: The mark separating whole units from tenths and smaller parts. Hundredth: One of 100 equal parts of one.

glossary.definition: The mark separating whole units from tenths and smaller parts.
One of 100 equal parts of one.

lessons.limits: The place-value rule applies to decimal numbers. Keep the measurement unit when the number describes a quantity.

focus.idea: A decimal can name parts smaller than one.
focus.explanation: The first place after the decimal point counts tenths. The next counts hundredths. One hundredth is one of 100 equal parts of one.

One of 100 equal parts of one.

explanations: Yes. The 7 is in the hundredths place.
Seven tenths is 0.7. Here the tenths place is zero.
0.07 is smaller than one; it contains 7 hundredths.

lessons.title: Move along a number line
lessons.idea: Adding a positive number moves you right along the number line.
body: Negative numbers are to the left of zero. Start at the first number, then count right when you add a positive amount. You may reach zero or pass it.

equationGuide.meaning: Negative numbers are to the left of zero. Start at the first number, then count right when you add a positive amount. You may reach zero or pass it.

example.title: A warmer temperature
steps: A thermometer reads −3 °C.
It warms by 2 degrees: count right from −3 to −2, then to −1.
The new reading is −1 °C.

lessons.terms: Negative number: A number less than zero. Number line: A line where numbers increase as you move right.

glossary.definition: A number less than zero.
A line where numbers increase as you move right.

lessons.limits: This lesson adds a positive amount. A negative Celsius reading does not mean a negative absolute temperature.

focus.idea: Adding a positive number moves you right along the number line.

check.prompt: Start at −2 and add 3. Where do you finish?
explanations: Adding a positive amount moves right, toward larger numbers.

lessons.title: Read percent as out of a hundred
lessons.idea: Percent means out of a hundred.
body: Divide a percentage by 100 to write it as a decimal. Multiply that decimal by the whole amount to find the chosen part.

equationGuide.meaning: Divide a percentage by 100 to write it as a decimal. Multiply that decimal by the whole amount to find the chosen part.

example.title: A share of 50 counters
steps: You want 20% of a group of 50 counters.
20% is 0.20, so the share is 0.20 × 50 = 10 counters.

lessons.terms: Percent (%): An amount out of 100. Whole amount: The full amount from which a share is taken.

glossary.definition: An amount out of 100.
The full amount from which a share is taken.

lessons.limits: The percentage must refer to a stated whole. A percentage change and a change in percentage points are different questions.

focus.idea: Percent means out of a hundred.
focus.explanation: Divide a percentage by 100 to write it as a decimal. Multiply that decimal by the whole amount to find the chosen part.

terms.definition: An amount out of 100.
The full amount from which a share is taken.

explanations: Divide the percentage by 100.
0.5 is 50 out of 100.

lessons.title: Work inside brackets first
lessons.idea: Brackets tell you which calculation belongs together.
body: Complete the calculation inside a pair of brackets before using its result outside. This keeps the intended grouping clear.

equationGuide.meaning: Complete the calculation inside a pair of brackets before using its result outside. This keeps the intended grouping clear.

example.title: Two matching bags
steps: Each bag has 3 red counters and 4 blue counters. There are 2 bags.
One bag contains 3 + 4 = 7 counters.
The two bags contain 2 × 7 = 14 counters.

lessons.terms: Brackets ( ): Marks that group a part of a calculation.

glossary.definition: Marks that group a part of a calculation.

lessons.limits: Work from inner brackets outward when brackets are nested. Outside brackets, powers come before multiplication/division, then addition/subtraction.

focus.idea: Brackets tell you which calculation belongs together.
focus.explanation: Complete the calculation inside a pair of brackets before using its result outside. This keeps the intended grouping clear.

check.prompt: In 3 × (2 + 5), what should you calculate first?
explanations: First finish the grouped calculation inside the brackets.
Yes. The brackets group 2 + 5.
The expression asks for multiplication outside the brackets.

lessons.title: Read a power as repeated multiplication
lessons.idea: A power such as 3² tells you how many matching numbers to multiply.
body: In 3², the small 2 tells us to multiply two 3s. It counts copies of 3 in the multiplication.

equationGuide.meaning: In 3², the small 2 tells us to multiply two 3s. It counts copies of 3 in the multiplication.

example.title: A square of counters
steps: Arrange 3 rows with 3 counters in each row.
There are 3 × 3 = 9 counters. We can write this as 3².

lessons.terms: Base: The number being multiplied. Exponent: The small raised number that tells how many factors to use here. Squared: Raised to the power 2.

glossary.definition: The number being multiplied.
The small raised number that tells how many factors to use here.
Raised to the power 2.

lessons.limits: This first rule describes positive whole-number exponents. Zero, negative and fractional exponents need their own definitions.

focus.idea: A power such as 3² tells you how many matching numbers to multiply.
focus.explanation: In 3², the small 2 tells us to multiply two 3s. It counts copies of 3 in the multiplication.

terms.definition: The number being multiplied.
The small raised number that tells how many factors to use here.

explanations: A power uses repeated multiplication.
The exponent counts the number of factors.
Yes. There are three factors, each equal to 2.

lessons.title: Undo a square
lessons.idea: The square-root sign asks for a number, zero or above, whose square gives the input.
body: Squaring multiplies a number by itself. Taking the square root reverses that step when the number is zero or above.

equationGuide.meaning: Squaring multiplies a number by itself. Taking the square root reverses that step when the number is zero or above.

example.title: Find a square’s side
steps: A square has an area of 36 square centimetres.
Its side is √36 = 6 centimetres, because 6 × 6 = 36.

lessons.terms: Square root (√): The nonnegative number that squares to the input. Nonnegative: Zero or greater.

glossary.definition: The nonnegative number that squares to the input.
Zero or greater.

lessons.limits: This lesson uses real square roots of nonnegative inputs. An equation such as x² = 36 also has a negative solution; the symbol √36 itself names the nonnegative root.

focus.idea: The square-root sign asks for a number, zero or above, whose square gives the input.
focus.explanation: Squaring multiplies a number by itself. Taking the square root reverses that step when the number is zero or above.

A square root answers “which number times itself gives this value?” The √ sign picks the zero or positive answer. For example, √9 = 3.

explanations: Yes. 4 × 4 = 16, and 4 is nonnegative.

lessons.title: Find the number that multiplies to one
lessons.idea: A number’s reciprocal multiplies with it to make one.
body: For a nonzero number, divide one by that number. This is useful when a rule asks you to divide by a quantity.

equationGuide.meaning: For a nonzero number, divide one by that number. This is useful when a rule asks you to divide by a quantity.

example.title: Undo a factor of four
steps: Start with the number 4. Its reciprocal is 1 ÷ 4 = 0.25.
Check it: 4 × 0.25 = 1.

lessons.terms: Reciprocal: One divided by a nonzero number.

glossary.definition: One divided by a nonzero number.

lessons.limits: Zero has no reciprocal. For a measured quantity, its reciprocal has the inverse unit, such as 1/s.

focus.idea: A number’s reciprocal multiplies with it to make one.
focus.explanation: For a nonzero number, divide one by that number. This is useful when a rule asks you to divide by a quantity.

lessons.title: Put a known value in place of a letter
lessons.idea: Put a known value in place of its letter to use a rule.
body: When a value is given, put it in place of its letter. Keep the operations in the rule, including brackets.

equationGuide.meaning: When a value is given, put it in place of its letter. Keep the operations in the rule, including brackets.

example.title: Three tickets
steps: Each ticket costs 2 coins. T is total cost and n is the number of tickets.
For 3 tickets, put 3 in place of n: T = 2 × 3.
The total cost is 6 coins.

lessons.terms: Substitute: Put a given value in place of a letter. T: The total number of coins in this example. n: The number of tickets in this example.

glossary.definition: Put a given value in place of a letter.
The total number of coins in this example.
The number of tickets in this example.

lessons.limits: Use values and units that fit the rule. A letter can mean different quantities in different lessons, so read its definition.

focus.idea: A letter in a rule can stand for a number.
focus.explanation: If one ticket costs two coins, the total cost depends on how many tickets you buy. Put that number in place of the letter in the rule. Then do the calculation.

example.title: Three tickets

The total number of coins in this example.

explanations: The rule asks for multiplication.

lessons.title: Read a function as an input rule
lessons.idea: A function gives one output for each allowed input.
body: The notation f(x) names the output of rule f for input x. Follow the rule to calculate that output.

equationGuide.meaning: The notation f(x) names the output of rule f for input x. Follow the rule to calculate that output.

example.title: Put three into the rule
steps: The rule doubles the input, then adds 1.
For input 3, doubling gives 6. Adding 1 gives output 7.

lessons.terms: Function: A rule assigning one output to each allowed input. Input: The value you put into the rule. Output: The value the rule gives back.

glossary.definition: A rule assigning one output to each allowed input.
The value you put into the rule.
The value the rule gives back.

lessons.limits: Some rules allow only certain inputs. For example, a denominator must not be zero. The domain is the set of allowed inputs.

lessons.title: Keep a fixed multiplier
lessons.idea: Two quantities are proportional when one is a fixed multiple of the other.
body: If the multiplier stays fixed, doubling the input doubles the output. The relationship must pass through zero: no input gives no output.

equationGuide.meaning: If the multiplier stays fixed, doubling the input doubles the output. The relationship must pass through zero: no input gives no output.

example.title: Buy twice as many tickets
steps: Tickets cost 3 coins each. Three tickets cost 9 coins.
Buying 6 tickets doubles the number of tickets, so the cost doubles to 18 coins.

lessons.terms: Proportional: Related by a fixed multiplier. Multiplier: The number used in a multiplication.

glossary.definition: Related by a fixed multiplier.
The number used in a multiplication.

lessons.limits: The ticket rule assumes a fixed price with no extra fee or discount. A rule with an added fixed amount is not direct proportionality.

lessons.title: Repeat the same multiplying step
lessons.idea: Exponential growth multiplies by the same factor each step.
body: The extra amount gets bigger when the starting amount gets bigger. Count how many multiplying steps occur, then use that count as the exponent.

equationGuide.meaning: The extra amount gets bigger when the starting amount gets bigger. Count how many multiplying steps occur, then use that count as the exponent.

example.title: Three rounds of doubling
steps: A game starts with 5 counters and doubles them each round.
After 3 rounds, the amount is 5 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 40 counters.

lessons.terms: Exponential growth: Growth using the same multiplier for each equal step. Factor: A number being multiplied.

glossary.definition: Growth using the same multiplier for each equal step.
A number being multiplied.

lessons.limits: This example uses whole rounds with an exactly fixed factor. A real population cannot be assumed to double forever.

focus.idea: Exponential growth multiplies by the same factor each step.

lessons.title: Ask which power makes the number
lessons.idea: A logarithm asks which exponent produces a number.
body: The small number beside log names the base. Ask which power of that base gives the number inside the brackets.

equationGuide.meaning: The small number beside log names the base. Ask which power of that base gives the number inside the brackets.

example.title: Find the missing power
steps: Ask: 2 raised to which power gives 8?
Since 2 × 2 × 2 = 8, the answer is 3. We write log₂(8) = 3.

lessons.terms: Logarithm (log): The exponent needed for a chosen base to give a number. Base: The number raised to a power. e: A fixed mathematical number, about 2.718. ln: A logarithm with base e.

glossary.definition: The exponent needed for a chosen base to give a number.
The number raised to a power.
A fixed mathematical number, about 2.718.
A logarithm with base e.

lessons.limits: A real logarithm needs a positive input and a positive base other than 1. Physics uses logarithms of unit-free ratios; first compare a measured quantity with a reference of the same unit.

focus.idea: A logarithm asks which exponent produces a number.

steps: Let n take the values 1, 2, 3 and 4.

lessons.title: Subtract the start from the finish
lessons.idea: A signed change is the final value minus the starting value.
body: The symbol Δ, called delta, means change. A positive answer means an increase in the chosen quantity. A negative answer means a decrease.
lessons.equation: Δx = final x − starting x = 7 m − 2 m = 5 m

equationGuide.meaning: The symbol Δ, called delta, means change. A positive answer means an increase in the chosen quantity. A negative answer means a decrease.

example.title: A cart changes position
steps: A cart starts at position 2 m and finishes at position 7 m on the same scale.
Its position change is 7 − 2 = 5 m.

lessons.terms: Δ (delta): A symbol meaning change in this lesson. Signed change: A difference that keeps its positive or negative sign.

glossary.definition: A symbol meaning change in this lesson.
A difference that keeps its positive or negative sign.

lessons.limits: Use the same reference and units for both values. Position change is not necessarily the total distance travelled.

focus.idea: A signed change is the final value minus the starting value.
focus.explanation: The symbol Δ, called delta, means change. A positive answer means an increase in the chosen quantity. A negative answer means a decrease.
focus.equation: Δx = final x − starting x = 7 m − 2 m = 5 m

example.title: A cart changes position
steps: A cart starts at position 2 m and finishes at position 7 m on the same scale.
Its position change is 7 − 2 = 5 m.

terms.definition: A symbol meaning change in this lesson.
A difference that keeps its positive or negative sign.

check.prompt: A value goes from 9 to 4. Which calculation gives its change?
explanations: Subtract the start from the finish, in that order.
Yes. The change is −5, showing a decrease.
Adding the readings does not find the change.
